AxisSettings Axis settings: how values are distributed across the axes, how the labels are formatted and shown, and the two axis captions. DataSettings Data settings: the graphs and reference lines the chart shows, its points buffer, and how playback fills the graphs. LegendSettings Legend settings: whether the legend is shown, which side it sits on, how it aligns, its offset from the plot, and its header and entry text styles. LineChart Root UI Toolkit control that draws one or more graph series with a grid, axis labels, a legend and point tooltips. The single public entry point of the package: author it in UXML or UI Builder, or drive it from code after calling Init(). articles/code-first/build-a-chart.html.title: Build a chart from code
articles/code-first/build-a-chart.html.keywords: Build a chart from code Goal: a LineChart created in C#, configured through its settings groups, initialized and added to a visual tree — showing the default graph. Prerequisites: the package is installed (Getting started) and you have a VisualElement to add the chart to (a UIDocument's rootVisualElement, or any container). Steps Create the control: new LineChart(). Nothing is drawn yet — the constructor only builds the element tree. Configure the groups you care about through the properties on the control. Each group is a plain object with documented properties; setting one applies it immediately: Grid, Axis, Legend, and so on. Call Init(). It builds the chart's model from what you configured and makes the control live. The explicit call matters because you are about to drive the chart from code: the playback methods (Play, Stop, Restart) throw on a chart that is not initialized, and a chart left to initialize itself does so only on the tick after it attaches to a panel — too late for the line that follows. The dataset methods (AddGraph and its siblings) are the exception: they record the change and take effect at Init(). Add the control to your tree. An initialized chart attaches without initializing again. If the control has to be in the tree before you are ready to call Init(), turn Advanced.AutoInitialize off so the tree does not initialize it for you. public static LineChart BuildAChart(VisualElement parent) { var chart = new LineChart(); chart.Grid.ColumnsRows = new Vector2Int(6, 4); chart.Legend.Side = LegendSide.Right; chart.Axis.XAxisCaption = "Time"; chart.Axis.YAxisCaption = "Value"; chart.Init(); parent.Add(chart); return chart; } Result A chart with a 6×4 grid, the legend to the right of the plot, "Time" and "Value" as axis captions, and the built-in default graph drawn across it — the placeholder every chart shows until it gets datasets of its own, the same one a LineChart dropped into UI Builder shows. A chart you only display does not need you to call Init() at all: with Advanced.AutoInitialize on (the default) it initializes itself when it attaches to a runtime panel, which is how the UXML-first track works. Next Feed data at runtime — replace the default graph with points your code produces. Datasets and data sources — what a graph description is and where its points come from.

articles/code-first/feed-data-at-runtime.title: Feed data at runtime
articles/code-first/feed-data-at-runtime.keywords: Feed data at runtime Goal: a graph whose points come from your code while the application runs — a Direct graph — added to an initialized chart. Prerequisites: an initialized LineChart (Build a chart from code). Steps Create a GraphDescription with ScriptableObject.CreateInstance. A description is the chart's unit of data: one series plus its line and point styling. Give it a name — the legend shows it. Code is just the quickest way for this guide: a description saved as an asset (Assets ▸ Create ▸ UI Line Chart ▸ Graph Description, Mode = Direct) works the same. Reference it from code and continue at step 3, or list it in the chart's Data group in UI Builder and only push. Probe in the Overview sample is such an asset. Switch it to Direct mode: set Mode to DataSourceMode.Direct. A Direct graph has no predefined source; it draws whatever you push. Add it to the chart with AddGraph. The chart starts drawing the new series immediately. Push points with Push. Each call appends one Vector2 (x, y); the chart reveals it according to its playback settings. public static GraphDescription FeedDataAtRuntime(LineChart chart) { var live = ScriptableObject.CreateInstance<GraphDescription>(); live.Name = "Live"; live.Mode = GraphDescription.DataSourceMode.Direct; chart.AddGraph(live); live.Push(new Vector2(0f, 0.5f)); live.Push(new Vector2(1f, 0.8f)); return live; } Result The chart draws a second series named "Live" with two points. Keep calling Push from your update loop, a timer or a network callback and the line grows. RemovePushedPoint and ClearPushedPoints edit what is already there; RemoveGraph takes the series off the chart. A Direct graph remembers at most PushedPointsHistoryLimit points; how many the chart draws is a separate setting, the points buffer in the Data group. Next Playback — how pushed and predefined points are revealed over time. Datasets and data sources — the predefined sources you can use instead of, or alongside, Direct graphs.

articles/concepts/datasets-and-data-sour.title: Datasets and data sources
articles/concepts/datasets-and-data-sour.keywords: Datasets and data sources What it is A chart draws descriptions: a GraphDescription is one series with its data and styling, a ReferenceLineDescription is one horizontal marker. Both are ScriptableObject assets, so the same description can sit on several charts and be edited in the Inspector; the chart's Data group lists which ones it shows. How it works A graph description is in one of two modes (DataSourceMode): Mode Where points come from Typical use Predefined one of six built-in sources, configured on the asset authored charts, previews, demos Direct Push calls from your code live data The predefined sources (PredefinedDataSource): Random — a random walk stepping along X; Manual — a hand-entered list of points; Curve — an AnimationCurve sampled into points; Waveform — a periodic wave (sine, square, triangle, sawtooth); File — points read from a JSON or CSV text asset; Derived — another graph transformed by an operation (moving average, change, total, derivative, integral). Derived graphs can chain: a derived graph may itself be the source of another. One property of a source matters beyond its shape: its Cardinality. A finite source produces a fixed number of points and stops; an infinite one keeps going from its X origin — Random and Waveform let you choose, and a Direct graph is infinite by nature. Playback treats the two differently, and the description reports the result as GraphDescription.Cardinality. When you edit a description, every chart showing it refreshes. Styling changes are applied in place. A change to the data itself — the mode, the source or one of its parameters — makes the chart reload that series; the chart tells the two apart by hashing the data settings, so only an edit that would change the produced points triggers a reload. What it is not A description stores the recipe for its points, not the points themselves. A predefined source generates them on demand from its parameters; a Direct graph keeps only a bounded history of what was pushed (PushedPointsHistoryLimit). How many points a chart draws is the chart's points buffer (PointsBufferLength, shared or per graph by PointsBufferMode), not a property of the description. Apply it Configure a predefined source from code exactly as the Inspector would: public static GraphDescription ConfigureAPredefinedSource() { var graph = ScriptableObject.CreateInstance<GraphDescription>(); graph.Name = "Wave"; graph.SelectedDataSource = GraphDescription.PredefinedDataSource.Waveform; graph.WaveformData.Shape = GraphDescription.WaveShape.Sine; graph.WaveformData.Frequency = 2f; graph.WaveformData.Amplitude = 0.5f; return graph; } See also Feed data at runtime — the Direct mode in practice. Add datasets — the same assets from UI Builder.

articles/concepts/playback.html.title: Playback
articles/concepts/playback.html.keywords: Playback What it is A chart does not necessarily show a dataset all at once. Its fill player reveals a graph's points over time — a finite source fills up and stops, an infinite or Direct one keeps flowing — according to the playback settings in the Data group. How it works The player ticks. Every tick it adds points to each playing graph: Setting Meaning Autoplay start filling on its own when the chart runs in play mode UpdateMode Continuous — points appear tick by tick; Immediate — all at once FillMode Fixed — PointsPerTick points each tick; Proportional — PercentPerTick of the data each tick TickRate seconds between ticks — smaller is faster From code you drive the same machinery per chart or per graph: Play, Stop, Restart (the int overloads take an index into Graphs), and IsPlaying to tell whether a graph is still filling. RevealFiniteImmediately shows every finite graph in full and skips the animation — it is what the chart does outside play mode so the editor preview is never empty. Playback methods need an initialized chart; before Init() they throw. What it is not TickRate is a period, not a frequency: 0.05 means a tick every 50 ms, twenty ticks a second. And playback is not the same as the points buffer — the buffer caps how many points are kept, playback decides how fast they appear. Apply it Take manual control: turn autoplay off, choose a fixed fill of two points every 100 ms, then start: public static void ControlPlayback(LineChart chart) { chart.Data.Autoplay = false; chart.Data.UpdateMode = GraphUpdateMode.Continuous; chart.Data.FillMode = FillMode.Fixed; chart.Data.PointsPerTick = 2; chart.Data.TickRate = 0.1f; chart.Play(); } See also Datasets and data sources — why finite and infinite sources fill differently. Feed data at runtime — pushed points go through the same player.

articles/concepts/scale.html.title: Scale
articles/concepts/scale.html.keywords: Scale What it is Advanced.Scale multiplies every chrome dimension of a chart — line and axis thicknesses, point sizes, offsets, dash widths and text size — and leaves the data alone. The default, 1, draws the chrome at exactly the pixels you authored. How it works When the chart writes its descriptions and settings into its model, each pixel value is multiplied by Scale; change Scale later and the chart writes them again. Text follows the same rule: a text style's font size is multiplied before it is applied. Two situations look similar and are not: Embedding — the chart is authored for the surface it appears on (a game HUD, an editor window). Thicknesses, sizes and offsets are per-chart settings, and every piece of text picks its style by key (see Text styles), so you set the values you want and Scale stays 1. It is not a shortcut for bigger text: a text style is the place for that, and Scale would drag lines, points and offsets along. Mirroring — a chart is shown as a smaller copy of another chart and must look like the original. Equal pixels in a narrower box read as heavier lines, so the copy needs previewWidth / referenceWidth folded into Scale. This is the one case where a computed value belongs, and Scale is what makes it expressible. The Overview sample does exactly this: LineChartPreviewer copies the runtime chart into the Inspector and into a window and sets each copy's Scale from its own width against the panel's reference resolution (see ComputePreviewScale in Samples/Overview/Runtime/LineChartPreviewer.cs), with a hand-picked readability boost for the narrow Inspector column. What it is not Scale does not compensate for screen resolution. That is the panel's job: with a PanelSettings scale mode such as Scale With Screen Size, UI Toolkit scales the whole visual tree, generated meshes included, and a 2 px line authored against a 1920 reference becomes 4 physical pixels on a 3840 screen without anyone touching Scale. Nor does it change the plotted range — axes and data are untouched. Apply it The mirroring case — a preview that must keep the original's visual weight: public static void MirrorAChart(LineChart preview, float previewWidth, float referenceWidth) { preview.Advanced.Scale = previewWidth / referenceWidth; } See also Text styles — where text size lives; a mirrored copy is the one case where Scale resizes text on the chart itself.

articles/concepts/text-styles.html.title: Text styles
articles/concepts/text-styles.html.keywords: Text styles What it is Every piece of text a chart draws — axis labels and captions, legend header and entries, the point tooltip and its projections, reference-line labels — is styled by key. The keys resolve against one project-wide asset, the TextStylesLibrary: a list of named TextStyleAttributes (font asset, size, color) plus a fallback style for unknown keys. How it works The library is a singleton resolved from Resources: the project's own TextStylesLibrary when there is one, otherwise the DefaultTextStylesLibrary the package ships. Charts do not own styles — they hold keys in their settings (XAxisLabelTextStyleKey, HeaderTextStyleKey, …), and every *TextStyleKey field in the Inspector is a dropdown over the library's keys. Change a style in the library and every chart using that key refreshes its text. Your project's library The package ships its styles as DefaultTextStylesLibrary, an asset inside the package that an installed package keeps read-only. A project overrides it with a TextStylesLibrary asset in any of its Resources folders. Tools ▸ UI Line Chart ▸ Open Text Styles Library opens that asset, or offers to create Assets/Resources/TextStylesLibrary.asset as a copy of the default when the project has none yet; the inspector of the default asset offers the same. The copy starts with the six keys every chart is authored against — AxisLabel, AxisCaption, LegendEntry, LegendHeader, ReferenceLineLabel, PointTooltip — so nothing changes until you edit a style or add a key of your own. Creating the copy reloads the scripts once, and from then on every chart resolves its keys against the project library. Resolution goes through TextStylesAttributes.Resolve: a known key returns its style; an unknown key logs an error and returns the FallbackStyle, so a typo never leaves text invisible. What it is not Text size is not a per-chart setting. Styles are shared, so a chart that needs bigger or smaller text points its *TextStyleKey fields at a different style rather than resizing anything on the chart itself. The one exception is a mirrored copy of another chart, where Scale shrinks or grows the text together with lines, points and offsets. Apply it Add a key to the library at runtime and point a chart's legend header at it: public static void PickATextStyle(LineChart chart) { var library = TextStylesLibrary.Instance; var baseStyle = library.Styles.Entries[0].Style; library.Styles.Set("legend-large", new TextStyleAttributes(baseStyle.Font, baseStyle.FontSize + 4, baseStyle.Color)); library.NotifyChanged(); chart.Legend.HeaderTextStyleKey = "legend-large"; } See also Scale — the one case where text is resized on the chart itself: a mirrored copy.

articles/getting-started.html.title: Getting started
articles/getting-started.html.keywords: Getting started UI Line Chart is a line chart control for UI Toolkit in Unity 6. It draws one or more graph series over a grid, with axis labels, a legend and a hover tooltip, and it has exactly one public entry point: the LineChart control. Everything else — grid, axes, legend, datasets, playback — is configured on it. Install The package depends on com.sxm-tools.ui-factory, published on OpenUPM. Add the scoped registry and the package to Packages/manifest.json: { "scopedRegistries": [ { "name": "package.openupm.com", "url": "https://package.openupm.com", "scopes": ["com.sxm-tools.ui-factory"] } ], "dependencies": { "com.sxm-tools.ui-line-chart": "https://github.com/sxm-sxpxxl/ui-line-chart.git" } } Unity resolves both packages on the next domain reload. Optional: import the Overview sample from the Package Manager window — every guide uses it as the reference result. What you get out of the box Drop a LineChart into a UXML document (or create one from code) and it already draws: a default graph generated by a built-in GraphDescription asset, a grid, both axes with value labels, and a legend. In UI Builder the control renders a live design-time preview of whatever it is configured to show, so you see the chart while you edit it. The control is configured through six settings groups, each a child element in UXML and a property in code: Grid, Axis, Data, Legend, PointTooltip and Advanced. Every field in every group shows its documentation as a tooltip in the Inspector and UI Builder — the same text you read in the API reference. Pick your track You can work with the chart entirely without code, or entirely from code, or mix the two. UXML-first — you author charts in UI Builder and describe data with GraphDescription assets. No C#. Start at Build a chart in UI Builder. Code-first — you create the control in C#, configure the settings groups, and push data at runtime. Start at Build a chart from code. Both tracks meet in the Concepts: how datasets and data sources work, how playback fills a graph, what Scale is for, and how text styles are shared across charts.

articles/known-issues.html.title: Known issues
articles/known-issues.html.keywords: Known issues Problems you may meet while working with the chart, what causes them and how to work around them. They are Unity Editor behaviors, not chart defects, and the package cannot switch them off for you. UI Builder lags and logs EndLayoutGroup errors while you edit a chart Symptom. Dragging a numeric field of a chart in UI Builder (a thickness, an offset, the grid size) stutters, and the Console fills with EndLayoutGroup: BeginLayoutGroup must be called first — one error per change. The lag grows with the number of Inspector tabs, Game views and charts on screen. Cause. UI Toolkit Live Reload. Every UI Builder edit, saved or not, changes the document asset in memory, and every window with Live Reload on reacts to it: An Inspector tab (Live Reload is off by default for editor windows, but the switch is easy to leave on) recreates its whole window on each change. The error is that recreation happening in the middle of a layout pass; a stock inspector such as a Transform or a Camera produces it just the same. A Game view (Live Reload is on by default for the runtime) re-clones the document's UI on each change, so every chart in it is created and initialized again. Live Reload works at the window level; the chart cannot opt out of it. Workaround. While you edit in UI Builder, turn UI Toolkit Live Reload off in the ⋮ menu of the Inspector tab and of the Game tab. The switch applies to all windows of the same type. The UI Builder canvas keeps showing the chart live; the other windows stop mirroring every change. Alternatively keep the Inspector and Game tabs hidden behind other tabs while you scrub. See UI Toolkit live reload in the Unity Manual for the details of the feature.

articles/uxml-first/add-datasets.html.title: Add datasets
articles/uxml-first/add-datasets.html.keywords: Add datasets Goal: the chart draws two graphs and one reference line, all described by assets you create in the Project window — still no C#. Prerequisites: a chart in UI Builder (Build a chart in UI Builder). Steps Choose Assets ▸ Create ▸ UI Line Chart ▸ Graph Description and name the asset. It is a GraphDescription: one series, its data source and its line/point styling. Select the asset. Under Data Source pick a predefined source — start with Waveform — and tune it; the Inspector explains each field and shows a formula card for the source. Create a second graph the same way. Assets ▸ Create ▸ UI Line Chart ▸ Reference Line Description makes a ReferenceLineDescription for a horizontal marker; set its Y Reference Value. Back in UI Builder, select the chart, open the Data group (DataSettings) and drag your two graph assets into Graphs and the reference line into Reference Lines. The preview draws them. Save. The Data group is written with project:// references to the assets: <ui:UXML xmlns:ui="UnityEngine.UIElements" editor-extension-mode="False"> <SxmTools.UILineChart.View.LineChart name="line-chart" style="flex-grow: 1;"> <SxmTools.UILineChart.View.DataSettings graphs="project://database/Packages/com.sxm-tools.ui-line-chart/Samples/Overview/Data/Measured.asset?fileID=11400000&guid=18203195064ec91439b52ac2ca8f362e&type=2#Measured,project://database/Packages/com.sxm-tools.ui-line-chart/Samples/Overview/Data/Forecast.asset?fileID=11400000&guid=790794a5306e5624985b9cd57bba0309&type=2#Forecast" reference-lines="project://database/Packages/com.sxm-tools.ui-line-chart/Samples/Overview/Data/Comfort.asset?fileID=11400000&guid=79249e3d05fb2a2448ae2696dc13a2e3&type=2#Comfort"/> </SxmTools.UILineChart.View.LineChart> </ui:UXML> Result Two series and a horizontal reference line, each named in the legend. Change an asset later — a color, a frequency — and every chart that references it updates, in the editor preview and at runtime. articles/uxml-first/build-a-chart.html.title: Build a chart in UI Builder
articles/uxml-first/build-a-chart.html.keywords: Build a chart in UI Builder Goal: a chart authored entirely in UI Builder — grid and legend configured, live preview showing the default graph — with no C#. Prerequisites: the package is installed (Getting started) and a UXML document is open in UI Builder. Steps In the Library, find LineChart under the package's namespace and drag it into the hierarchy. The canvas shows the chart at once — the control renders a design-time preview in the editor. Select the chart. Its Inspector shows six foldouts, one per settings group. Open Grid (GridSettings) click the Columns Rows grid to pick 6 columns by 4 rows, and set Axis Stroke to Solid. The preview redraws as you type. Open Legend (LegendSettings) and set Side to Right. Hover any field to read what it does — every field carries the same documentation you find in the API reference. Save. UI Builder writes each configured group as a child element of the chart, with only the values that differ from the defaults. This is the UXML UI Builder produces: <ui:UXML xmlns:ui="UnityEngine.UIElements" editor-extension-mode="False"> <SxmTools.UILineChart.View.LineChart name="line-chart" style="flex-grow: 1;"> <SxmTools.UILineChart.View.GridSettings columns-rows="6,4" axis-stroke="Solid"/> <SxmTools.UILineChart.View.LegendSettings side="Right"/> </SxmTools.UILineChart.View.LineChart> </ui:UXML> Result A chart with a 6×4 solid grid and the legend to the right of the plot, drawing the built-in default graph. In a runtime UIDocument it initializes itself on attach — nothing to call. Next Add datasets — replace the default graph with your own data assets.
